title_en: On the Parts of the Soul
author: John of Damascus
occasion: A brief doctrinal summary of the soul's parts, virtues, law, and faculties, apparently compiled for instruction or reference.
argument: The soul has three parts: appetitive, spirited, and rational (or logical). The most sacred mind is enthroned on four virtues: understanding, courage, justice, and temperance. The law is threefold: natural, written, and spiritual in grace. The body is fourfold like a cosmos, while the soul is tripartite, prefiguring the Holy Trinity and giving life through its activities. This appetitive part is divided into three: divine, natural, and middle/fleshly, which is the diabolical. The soul also has five powers: intellect, discursive thought, opinion, imagination, and sense perception.

outline.move: States the three parts of the soul, the four virtues enthroning the most sacred mind, the threefold law, the fourfold body, and the tripartite soul prefiguring the Holy Trinity and giving life through its activities, with the functions of each soul-part specified.

Divides the appetitive part into divine, natural, and middle/fleshly (which is diabolical), with examples of what is according to nature and what is contrary to nature, and notes the material was found in another source.
Introduces the five powers of the soul and defines intellect (νοῦς) as intellectual perception of the soul by which it is able to see things with direct vision and without inquiries.

Defines discursive thought as the power by which the soul knows things with reasoning, opinion as the power by which it knows things without cause, imagination as a power of the irrational soul, and sense perception as the power apprehending material things.

key_terms.sense: The appetitive or desiring part of the soul, which loves or desires.
The spirited or irascible part of the soul, by which one is angry with demons and acts courageously.
The rational or reasoning part of the soul, by which one reasons.
The intellect or mind, the soul's intellectual perception by which it sees things directly.
Discursive thought, the power of knowing things through reasoning.
Opinion, the power of knowing things without cause or demonstration.
Imagination, a power of the non-rational soul.
Sense perception, the soul's power of apprehending material things.
The four cardinal virtues on which the mind is enthroned.
The law in its threefold form: natural, written, and spiritual in grace.
The fleshly or diabolical kind of desire, which loves what is contrary to nature.

_unresolved_facts.claim: The most sacred mind is enthroned on four virtues: understanding, courage, justice, and temperance
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Ἀρεταῖς δὲ τέσσαρσι τεθρόνισται ὁ ἱερώτατος νοῦς· φρονήσεως, ἀνδρείας, δικαιοσύνης, σωφροσύνης
_unresolved_facts.fix: The most sacred mind is enthroned by four virtues: prudence (φρονήσεως), courage/fortitude (ἀνδρείας), justice (δικαιοσύνης), and temperance (σωφροσύνης)

_unresolved_facts.claim: The soul has three parts: appetitive, spirited, and rational (or logical)
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Τῆς δὲ ψυχῆς μέρη γʹ. Ἐπιθυμητικὸν, θυμικόν, λογιστικόν... Τριμερῆ δὲ λέγομεν τὴν ψυχήν, ἔχουσαν λογικὸν, θυμικόν, καὶ ἐπιθυμητικόν
_unresolved_facts.fix: The soul has three parts: appetitive (ἐπιθυμητικόν), spirited/irascible (θυμικόν), and rational (λογιστικόν in the first instance, λογικόν in the second). Note: the source uses both λογιστικόν and λογικόν, not consistently 'rational (or logical)'

_unresolved_facts.fix: with the functions of the rational and spirited parts specified (the appetitive part's function is not specified in u01-open, only that it loves God)
